the effect of skew on the transaction response is a combination of the effects of skew on data contention and on the buffer hit probability; and that the buffer hit probability is a function of the skew distribution, which can be broken down to multiple regions.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for skewed data access, the buffer hit probability increases with skew and the response time decreases with skew, but the effect on the response time depends on the CC protocol and the access frequency distribution of data granules.

the effect of skew in data access depends on the system parameters, CC protocols, and the buffer hit probability, but that in general, skew does not lead to worse performance and optimistic CC is more effective than pessimistic CC.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for a data sharing environment with skewed data access, optimistic concurrency control (CC), which is more robust than the pessimistic CC, can be made more effective by allocating more buffer to the system with the higher access frequency, and by allocating a smaller buffer to each system.
, in the context of a multisystem data-sharing environment, skewness in data access has an impact on performance, but the effect is not always negative.
the effect of skewed data access is to increase the buffer hit ratio.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the performance of a multisystem data-sharing environment with skewed data access is a complex function of the skewness, concurrency control, and buffer size.
the performance of a multisystem environment with skew is not necessarily worse than that of a system with uniform data access, and the performance of the two environments can be comparable.
, for the case where the skewness is not too high, the buffer hit probability can be improved by allocating more local buffer space.
